title: Simulacro 06 — Container security y registries
focus: Image scanning (Trivy, Grype). SBOM (Syft). Signature verification (cosign, Sigstore). Private registries (Harbor, ECR). Image pull secrets. Image immutability. Base image selection. Runtime security (Falco). CVE management. Todo lo que un container debe pasar antes de correr en prod.

questions.scenario: Un dev jr pregunta: '¿dónde están las Docker images? ¿En mi laptop? ¿En Docker?'.
questions.question: ¿Qué es un container registry?

options.text: Container registry: servicio que almacena y distribuye container images. 'docker push' sube image al registry; 'docker pull' baja. Registries famosos: Docker Hub (default, público), AWS ECR (Elastic Container Registry), Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry (ACR), GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), Harbor (self-hosted), JFrog Artifactory. Cada image tiene: repository name, tag (v1.0, latest), digest (SHA256). Registries pueden ser públicos o privados con auth.
options.why: Correcto. Registries son 'source of truth' para container images. Sin registry, no puedes deploy en otra máquina que no tenga la image built localmente.

options.text: Un container registry es un container.
options.why: Confusión. Un registry es un SERVICIO que sirve images. Puede correr en un container él mismo (Harbor, Docker Registry) pero conceptualmente son diferentes.

options.text: Las Docker images están en tu laptop siempre.
options.why: Falso — están en tu laptop CUANDO las pulls. Se almacenan cache local. Pero fuente original es el registry.

options.text: Docker es un registry.
options.why: Docker es la plataforma. Docker HUB es el registry público que Docker Inc opera. Confusión común.

questions.explanation:
Registry conceptos: (1) REPOSITORY — nombre de una image (ej. 'myapp'). Contiene múltiples tags/versions. (2) TAG — nombre humano (v1.0, latest, prod). Mutable — puede reasignarse a distinta image. (3) DIGEST — SHA256 hash del image manifest. INMUTABLE. Formato: sha256:abc123... (4) MANIFEST — JSON con metadata + layer references. (5) LAYERS — binary blobs del image.

Registry types: (a) Public — Docker Hub, quay.io, gcr.io (public repos). Anyone can pull. Free tier limits (Docker Hub 100 pulls/6h anonymous). (b) Private — same providers con auth. Solo authorized users pull/push. (c) Self-hosted — Harbor, JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, distribution/distribution (open source Docker Registry). (d) Cloud provider — ECR (AWS), Artifact Registry (GCP), ACR (Azure), GHCR (GitHub).

Auth: (a) Docker Hub — username/password, personal access token. (b) ECR — AWS IAM. (c) GHCR — GitHub personal access token, GitHub Actions token. (d) Harbor — user accounts, robot accounts, OIDC integration.

Pull/Push commands:
```bash
docker login docker.io
docker pull nginx:1.25
docker tag myapp:1.0 myorg/myapp:1.0
docker push myorg/myapp:1.0
```

OCI Distribution Spec: standard API para registries (get manifest, get blob, put manifest, put blob). Docker Registry v2 → OCI Distribution. Tools like skopeo, crane usan OCI API directamente sin daemon.

Cost model: (1) Docker Hub — free public, paid private tiers. (2) ECR — $0.10/GB/month storage + bandwidth. (3) GHCR — free para public y private (with limits). (4) Self-hosted — infra cost.
questions.realWorld: Docker Hub was FIRST public registry (2013). En 2020, Docker Hub introduced pull rate limits (100/6h anon, 200 authenticated) que causó incidents en muchas CIs que pull frecuentemente. En 2021, Docker Hub removed some inactive images causando confusion. Cloud providers grew registries: ECR, GCR, ACR. Harbor (CNCF Graduated) popular self-hosted enterprise choice.

questions.scenario: Tu security team te envía: 'CVE-2021-44228 CRITICAL en tu image'. Un dev jr pregunta qué significa 'CVE'.
questions.question: ¿Qué es una CVE?

options.text: CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures): identificador estándar de una vulnerabilidad de seguridad conocida. Format: CVE-YYYY-NNNN (año-numero). Maintained by MITRE. Cada CVE tiene: description, affected products/versions, severity score (CVSS), references. Herramientas de scanning (Trivy, Grype, Snyk) escanean tus dependencies/images contra CVE database y reportan matches. Ejemplo famoso: CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) — remote code execution en Log4j.
options.why: Correcto. CVE es la 'lingua franca' de vulnerabilities. Cualquier tool serious references CVE IDs. NIST NVD (National Vulnerability Database) es la fuente principal.

options.text: CVE es un tipo de container.
options.why: Falso — CVE es identificador de vulnerabilidad, no de container.

options.text: CVE significa 'Container Vulnerability Explanation'.
options.why: Falso — 'Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures'. Existía antes de containers, aplica a cualquier software.

options.text: CVE es un producto de Docker.
options.why: Falso — CVE es un sistema abierto maintained por MITRE (nonprofit, US gov funded).

questions.explanation:
CVE lifecycle: (1) Discovery — vulnerability found (researcher, dev, attacker). (2) Report — reported to vendor + MITRE (responsible disclosure). (3) CVE ID reserved. (4) Fix released (patch). (5) Public disclosure — CVE published with details. (6) Databases updated (NVD, GHSA, OSV).

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System): (1) Base score 0.0-10.0. (2) Vector string encoding: AV (attack vector), AC (attack complexity), PR (privileges required), UI (user interaction), S (scope), C/I/A (confidentiality/integrity/availability impact). (3) Categorías: Critical (9.0-10.0), High (7.0-8.9), Medium (4.0-6.9), Low (0.1-3.9). (4) Environmental + temporal modifiers para adjust for your context.

Databases: (a) NVD — National Vulnerability Database (US NIST). Comprehensive. (b) GitHub Advisory Database (GHSA) — GitHub curated, integrates con Dependabot. (c) OSV — Open Source Vulnerabilities (Google). Standardized format for OSS. (d) Snyk DB. (e) OSS Index (Sonatype).

Example CVE: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228): CVSS 10.0. Log4j 2.0-2.14.1 vulnerable. Remote code execution via JNDI injection en log strings. December 2021 — one of the most impactful CVEs ever. Miles de empresas affected.

CVE + containers: image tiene multiple sources of CVEs: (1) Base OS (Alpine, Debian, Ubuntu) — apt/apk packages. (2) Language runtime (Node, Python, Java). (3) App dependencies (npm, pip, Maven). (4) System libraries (glibc, openssl). Todos scannables. Total CVEs por image típico: 10-500 con severity variados.

Management: (1) Prioritize por severity + exploitability. (2) Fix critical/high immediately. (3) Track medium/low with SLAs. (4) Some CVEs won't affect you (feature not used) — 'suppress' with justification. (5) Continuous monitoring — new CVEs discovered daily.
questions.realWorld: MITRE CVE program iniciado 1999. NVD launched 2005. Log4Shell (2021) marcó era — everyone rushed to update Log4j. Heartbleed (2014, CVE-2014-0160) OpenSSL famous. ShellShock (2014, CVE-2014-6271) bash. Spectre/Meltdown (2018) CPU-level. Recent: CVE-2023-38408 OpenSSH.

questions.scenario: Necesitas escanear tus Docker images en CI para bloquear deploys con vulnerabilidades críticas. Un ingeniero senior recomienda Trivy.
questions.question: ¿Qué es Trivy y cómo se usa?

options.text: Trivy (Aqua Security): scanner de vulnerabilidades open source. Escanea: (1) Container images — CVE en base OS + app deps; (2) Filesystems — codebase directly; (3) Git repos; (4) K8s clusters; (5) IaC (Terraform, K8s manifests). Fast, single binary, no daemon required. Actualmente scans: Node.js/npm, Python/pip, Ruby/gem, Java/Maven, Go modules, .NET NuGet, y OS packages (Alpine, Debian, RedHat, etc.). Comando: 'trivy image myimage:tag'. Exit code non-zero si vulnerabilities found — CI-friendly.
options.why: Correcto. Trivy es el scanner más popular open-source (2020+). Simple, rápido, comprehensive. Alternatives: Grype (Anchore), Snyk (SaaS), Docker Scout (Docker Inc).

options.text: Trivy es un runtime, corre containers.
options.why: Falso — Trivy es scanner (analiza images estáticamente), no runtime.

options.text: Trivy solo funciona para Docker Hub images.
options.why: Falso — escanea cualquier OCI image de cualquier registry (or local Docker daemon, or tar files).

options.text: Trivy es SaaS-only.
options.why: Falso — open source, single binary. Aqua tiene commercial version pero core es free.

questions.explanation:
Trivy usage:
```bash
# Scan image
trivy image nginx:1.25

# Only high/critical
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL nginx:1.25

# Fail if critical found (CI)
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL nginx:1.25

# JSON output for further processing
trivy image --format json nginx:1.25 > report.json

# Scan filesystem (dev)
trivy fs ./

# Scan K8s cluster
trivy k8s --report summary cluster

# Scan Terraform
trivy config .
```

Integración en CI (GitHub Actions):
```yaml
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: 'myapp:${{ github.sha }}'
    severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
    exit-code: '1'
    format: 'sarif'
    output: 'trivy.sarif'
- uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2
  with:
    sarif_file: 'trivy.sarif'
```
SARIF format uploads to GitHub Security tab.

Database: Trivy uses vulnerability database (updated daily). First scan downloads (large), subsequent uses cache. Airgapped env: pre-download DB.

Alternatives comparison: (1) Trivy — most popular open source, comprehensive. (2) Grype — Anchore, similar features, integrates con Syft (same vendor). (3) Snyk — SaaS + open source. Rich UX, PR integration. Paid. (4) Docker Scout — Docker Inc's offering. Integrated con Docker Desktop. Some free tier. (5) Anchore Enterprise — commercial full-featured. (6) Clair — CoreOS/RedHat, older, still used en Quay.

Gotchas: (1) False positives — CVE in a package no usado en runtime. Requires manual triage. (2) Vulnerability sin fix — 'noone has patched yet'. Options: accept risk, mitigate at network layer, replace package. (3) DB freshness — old scans miss new CVEs. (4) Container running old cached DB.
questions.realWorld: Trivy launched 2019 by Aqua Security. CNCF Sandbox 2022. Widely adopted en el ecosystem — Kubernetes, distros ship Trivy. Grype (Anchore) similar traction. GitHub Advanced Security integrates con Dependabot for similar functionality. Snyk popular en enterprise.

questions.scenario: Auditor de compliance pregunta: '¿qué dependencies EXACTAS están en tu container image?'. Nadie puede responder. ¿Qué es SBOM?
questions.question: ¿Qué es un SBOM y por qué es importante?

options.text: SBOM (Software Bill of Materials): inventory formal de TODOS los componentes de software en un artifact — dependencies directas y transitivas, versiones, licenses, hashes. Formatos: SPDX (Linux Foundation) y CycloneDX (OWASP). Herramientas para generar: Syft (Anchore), tern, cdxgen. Uso: (1) Audit — 'qué tengo en producción?'; (2) Vulnerability response — 'estamos afectados por Log4Shell?' — check SBOMs; (3) License compliance — 'usamos GPL?'; (4) Supply chain security — attestations firmadas de qué se buildeó.
options.why: Correcto. SBOM es fundamental en supply chain security moderno. US Executive Order 14028 (2021) mandó SBOM para federal software. NIST guidance, EU CRA (Cyber Resilience Act) similar mandates.

options.text: SBOM es solo para OSS.
options.why: Falso — igualmente importante en enterprise. Auditing propietario software requires SBOM.

options.text: SBOM es lo mismo que package.json.
options.why: package.json lista DIRECT deps. SBOM incluye TRANSITIVE deps y OS-level packages. Más completo y en formato estándar.

options.text: SBOM es un requerimiento nuevo sin base.
options.why: Falso — US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) established SBOM requirement para federal software. Now spreading globally.

questions.explanation:
SBOM contents típico: (1) Components — name, version, supplier, license, download URL, checksum. (2) Relationships — 'A depends on B'. (3) Metadata — creator, timestamp, target artifact. (4) Signatures/attestations optional.

Formats: (a) SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) — Linux Foundation. ISO standard. Verbose. (b) CycloneDX — OWASP. Focused on security use case. Lighter. (c) SWID tags — ISO/IEC 19770-2. Less common en OSS.

Generation:
```bash
# Syft: scan image
syft nginx:1.25 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
syft nginx:1.25 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cyclonedx.json

# Docker native (Docker Scout)
docker sbom nginx:1.25

# Trivy also generates SBOMs
trivy image --format spdx-json --output sbom.json nginx:1.25
```

Use cases: (1) Vulnerability response — 'new CVE en package X, are we affected?' Query SBOMs. (2) License audit — 'what licenses do we use? Any AGPL?'. (3) Supply chain integrity — attestation firmada dice 'este binary fue buildeado desde este SBOM' — verifiable chain. (4) Compliance — SOX, FedRAMP, EU CRA todos moving to SBOM requirements.

Storage/distribution: (1) SBOM inline en image (OCI artifact). Modern tools support. (2) SBOM as separate artifact en registry. (3) Sigstore/Rekor — transparency log for SBOMs + signatures. (4) SBOM in release artifacts en GitHub Releases.

Attestation: SBOM + signature = attestation. 'I certify this SBOM represents the components of this artifact'. cosign attest verifies.

SPDX vs CycloneDX: (1) SPDX — ISO/IEC 5962:2021 standard. Detailed license focus. Government/regulated. (2) CycloneDX — Security-focused. Simpler. Fast adoption. Both widely supported by tools.
questions.realWorld: US EO 14028 (Biden, May 2021) mandó SBOM para federal software. NIST NTIA published minimum elements. NSA/CISA published SBOM guidance 2023. Log4Shell (Dec 2021) accelerated adoption — organizations que no tenían SBOMs took weeks to identify affected systems. EU CRA (2024) similar requirement. Syft, Trivy, Docker Scout all support SBOM generation.

questions.scenario: Tu K8s cluster pulls images de un registry. Un attacker con acceso al registry sustituye una image con backdoor. K8s pulls la fake. ¿Cómo verificar authenticity?
questions.question: ¿Qué es cosign y cómo enable signature verification?

options.text: cosign (Sigstore project): tool para SIGN y VERIFY container images (y otros OCI artifacts). Sign con private key (o keyless con OIDC). Signature stored en registry as sibling artifact. Verify checks signature against public key/OIDC identity. K8s admission controllers (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, Connaisseur) pueden rechazar images unsigned. Ecosystem: Rekor (transparency log), Fulcio (CA para keyless).
options.why: Correcto. Sigstore/cosign es el standard emergente. Simplifies signing dramatically vs prior tools (Notary v1). Widely adopted 2022+.

options.text: cosign es un runtime alternative.
options.why: Falso — signing tool, no runtime.

options.text: Docker verifies images automáticamente sin config.
options.why: Falso — by default no signature verification. Needs explicit setup.

options.text: cosign es propietario de Docker Inc.
options.why: Falso — Sigstore es Linux Foundation project. Vendor-neutral.

questions.explanation:
cosign workflows:

Key-based signing:
```bash
# Generate key pair
cosign generate-key-pair
# → cosign.key (private), cosign.pub (public)

# Sign
cosign sign --key cosign.key myorg/app:v1.0
# Password prompt

# Verify
cosign verify --key cosign.pub myorg/app:v1.0
```

Keyless (OIDC) signing:
```bash
# Sign with GitHub OIDC (no local key)
cosign sign myorg/app:v1.0
# Opens browser for OIDC login
# Signature includes GitHub identity claim
# Recorded en Rekor transparency log

# Verify with expected identity
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity=user@example.com \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer=https://accounts.google.com \
  myorg/app:v1.0
```

CI signing (GitHub Actions):
```yaml
- uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
- run: cosign sign --yes ${{ env.IMAGE }}
  env:
    COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL: 1
  # OIDC token from GHA authorizes signing
```

Sigstore ecosystem: (1) cosign — CLI. (2) Fulcio — free CA. Issues short-lived certs based on OIDC. (3) Rekor — transparency log (write-only, immutable). Records all signings. (4) Public Good Instance — free for OSS.

K8s admission control:
```yaml
# Kyverno policy
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-signed-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
    - name: verify-image
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["myorg/*"]
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: "user@example.com"
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
```

Attestations: cosign attest signs statements ABOUT images: (1) SBOM. (2) Vulnerability scan results. (3) Build provenance (SLSA). Verifiable claims.

Notary v1 (DCT — Docker Content Trust): older signing. Complex UX. Rarely used. cosign es successor.
questions.realWorld: Sigstore launched 2021 (Linux Foundation, Google, Red Hat, others). GitHub uses Sigstore para npm signing (2023+). Kubernetes core images signed with cosign. Chainguard Images all signed. In 2022, ArtifactHub started requiring signatures for verified publishers. SolarWinds attack (2020) accelerated interest en signing.

questions.scenario: Tu empresa no quiere images en Docker Hub público. Necesita private registry. Un ingeniero menciona Harbor.
questions.question: ¿Qué es Harbor y por qué usar private registry?

options.text: Harbor (CNCF Graduated): open source enterprise registry. Features: RBAC (users, groups, projects), replication entre instances, image signing integration (cosign, Notary), vulnerability scanning integrado (Trivy), image immutability policies, quotas por project, garbage collection, auditability. Alternative a paid enterprise registries (JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, docker Trusted Registry). Self-hosted → data sovereignty. Popular en enterprise.
options.why: Correcto. Harbor es el líder open source enterprise registry. VMware/Broadcom originally. CNCF Graduated 2020. Widely used en enterprise K8s environments.

options.text: Harbor es un tipo de container runtime.
options.why: Falso — registry, no runtime.

options.text: Harbor solo funciona con VMware.
options.why: Falso — originally from VMware pero open source, cross-platform.

options.text: Private registries no ofrecen ventajas.
options.why: Falso — ventajas: security (no public exposure), performance (local), compliance (data residency), cost control, feature control.

questions.explanation:
Por qué private registry: (1) SECURITY — images no publicly accessible. Attacker can't see what versions you run. (2) COMPLIANCE — data residency requirements (EU GDPR, US FedRAMP). Some countries require data stay in country. (3) PERFORMANCE — local pull faster than external. Reduces bandwidth costs, cold start times. (4) RELIABILITY — no dependence on Docker Hub uptime + rate limits. (5) CONTROL — pruning policies, retention rules, quotas per team. (6) SUPPLY CHAIN — mirror external images (npm, apt) para prevent public dependency changes.

Harbor features detail: (1) PROJECTS — logical grouping. Users tienen permissions per project. (2) REPLICATION — sync images between Harbor instances o external registries. Multi-region setups. (3) IMMUTABILITY — 'v1.0.0 no puede overwrite'. Optional per project. (4) TAG RETENTION — 'keep last 10 tags, delete older'. Auto GC. (5) SCANNING — Trivy scan on push. Block deploys si CVEs critical. (6) SIGNATURES — Notary v1 + cosign. (7) RBAC — fine-grained. (8) OIDC — SSO integration. (9) WEBHOOKS — notifications on events.

Alternatives: (a) Distribution/distribution (Docker Registry) — open source, minimal. No UI, no RBAC. Bare bones. (b) JFrog Artifactory — commercial, multi-artifact (Maven, npm, Docker, Helm, etc.). (c) Sonatype Nexus — similar, popular. (d) Cloud native — ECR (AWS), Artifact Registry (GCP), ACR (Azure), GHCR (GitHub). (e) Quay (Red Hat) — commercial + open source (Project Quay). (f) GitLab Container Registry — integrated with GitLab.

Deployment: Harbor via Helm chart o docker-compose. HA multi-node setups. Persistent storage (S3, NFS, local). Typical resources: 3 nodes, 100GB storage minimum, grows con images.

Mirror pattern: config Harbor como proxy cache para public registries. 'pull docker.io/nginx' → Harbor pulls y caches → subsequent pulls fast + no rate limits.
questions.realWorld: Harbor started 2016 (VMware), open sourced. CNCF Sandbox 2018, Graduated 2020. Widely used en telco, banking, government K8s deployments. In 2019, Docker Hub introduced rate limits — accelerated adoption of registry mirrors. JFrog IPO 2020. Alternatives like Chainguard (2022+) reimagining registry space.

questions.scenario: Tu K8s cluster necesita pull images de un private registry. K8s ni sabe las credentials.
questions.question: ¿Cómo se configuran image pull secrets en Kubernetes?

options.text: Image pull secret: K8s Secret de tipo 'kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson' que contiene credenciales del registry. Se crea con 'kubectl create secret docker-registry' o desde manifest. Se referencia en Pod spec con 'imagePullSecrets: [name: myregistry-secret]'. K8s presents credentials al pull image. Alternative: (1) ServiceAccount con imagePullSecret asociado — Pods usando ese SA heredan. (2) Node-level credentials — kubelet configured con registry auth (menos common). (3) Cloud provider integration (ECR IAM en EKS).
options.why: Correcto. Pattern estándar. kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson matches el format del ~/.docker/config.json.

options.text: Cluster K8s reads credentials del pod filesystem.
options.why: Falso — Secret separado, K8s los presenta al container runtime.

options.text: K8s no soporta private registries.
options.why: Falso — soportado nativamente.

options.text: Hardcode credentials en el Dockerfile.
options.why: Falso — expone credentials al mundo. Anti-patrón crítico.

questions.explanation:
Creation:
```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry myregistry \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=user \
  --docker-password='xxx' \
  --docker-email=user@example.com
```

Use in Pod:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: myregistry
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.example.com/myorg/app:v1
```

Use via ServiceAccount:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp-sa
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: myregistry
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: myapp-sa
  # imagePullSecrets inherited
```

Cloud-specific: (1) EKS — IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) + ECR. No static credentials. IAM policy gives ECR pull. (2) GKE — Workload Identity + Artifact Registry. Similar. (3) AKS — Managed Identity + ACR. (4) On-prem — usually static secrets.

Credential rotation: (1) Static secrets — rotate manually. (2) IAM/Workload Identity — no static secrets, automatic. (3) Robot accounts en Harbor — long-lived tokens with limited scope.

Multiple registries: cada registry needs its own secret. Or use auth helper (docker credential-helper) que fetches from vault/aws.

Anti-patterns: (1) Committing secret manifest to Git plaintext — anyone can decode base64. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, External Secrets Operator. (2) Cluster-wide default secret — over-permissive. Use per-namespace. (3) Long-lived tokens — should rotate. (4) Sharing secret across teams — blast radius.

OCI Distribution auth: (1) Basic auth — username/password. (2) Bearer token — OAuth2. (3) Cloud IAM — for AWS/GCP/Azure. (4) K8s ServiceAccount JWT — some registries support (kubelet oidc-issuer).
questions.realWorld: Standard K8s pattern. Sealed Secrets (Bitnami, 2017) para encrypt secrets in Git. External Secrets Operator (2020+) para bridge to Vault/AWS Secrets. In 2020, GitHub Actions ECR OIDC federation became popular — no static credentials. Chainguard Enforce for K8s admission based on signatures.

questions.scenario: Un dev push image myapp:v1.0. Luego push distinta image con el mismo tag myapp:v1.0. Ahora ambientes que pulled v1.0 en distintos momentos tienen DIFERENTES images. Caos.
questions.question: ¿Qué es image immutability y cómo enforce?

options.text: Image immutability: una vez pushed una image con tag específico, ese tag NO puede reasignarse a otra image. Fuerza push a nueva versión (v1.1) para cambios. Beneficios: (1) reproducibility — mismo tag = mismo binary siempre; (2) rollback confiable — kubectl rollout undo funciona sin ambigüedad; (3) audit — 'v1.0' es históricamente identificable. Enforcement: (a) Registry policy (Harbor, Docker Hub premium, ECR); (b) Pin por digest en producción (image@sha256:abc) — inmutable by cryptography; (c) Semantic versioning discipline — never republish version.
options.why: Correcto. Immutability es fundamental production principle. Sin ella, 'v1.0 en dev' puede ser distinto 'v1.0 en prod' — pesadilla debugging.

options.text: Tags mutables son ventaja siempre.
options.why: Falso — mutability creates ambiguity. Latest funcionamiento es útil para dev, terrible para prod.

options.text: K8s previene esto automáticamente.
options.why: Falso — K8s pulls la image cuando starts. Si el registry ha reassigned el tag, K8s pulls la nueva. Nada previene si registry allows overwrite.

options.text: Solo aplica a public registries.
options.why: Falso — importante en cualquier registry. Enterprise usually MORE strict sobre this.

questions.explanation:
Immutability enforcement layers: (1) REGISTRY LEVEL — Harbor 'Tag immutability rules' (per project). ECR 'ImmutableRepository' setting. Docker Hub Pro. Prevents overwrite en source. (2) DEPLOYMENT LEVEL — pin por digest en manifests/Helm. 'image@sha256:abc123...' — mathematically immutable. (3) PROCESS LEVEL — release process never republishes existing version. Bump semver siempre.

Digest vs tag: (a) Tag — human-readable, mutable. 'myapp:v1.0'. (b) Digest — SHA256 hash of manifest. 'myapp@sha256:abc123...'. Immutable — same digest = exact same content, byte-for-byte.

Best practice production K8s:
```yaml
containers:
  - name: app
    image: myorg/app@sha256:abc123def456...  # digest, no tag
```
CI updates the digest on new deploys.

GitOps integration: Argo CD, Flux support pin by digest. Renovate/Dependabot pattern to update digest on new versions.

Tag mutability use cases: (a) 'latest' — always latest push. Convenient dev, avoid prod. (b) 'main' — always tip of main branch. Similar. (c) semantic versioning (v1.0.0) — should be IMMUTABLE. (d) 'v1' or 'v1.0' — moving pointers. Convenient con caveats.

ECR example:
```json
{
  "imageTagMutability": "IMMUTABLE"
}
```
Once set, tags cannot be overwritten. Force new tags for updates.

Harbor policy: Configurable per project. Rules: 'tag matches pattern' + 'ignore N most recent'. Fine-grained control.

Audit case: 'deploy incident 3 días atrás, imagen v1.5 falló. Rollback a v1.4. Ahora nueva v1.5 funciona. Root cause? Si tags mutables, la v1.5 fallida puede haber sido sobrescrita, cannot investigate'. Immutability preserves forensics.
questions.realWorld: Netflix Spinnaker enforces digest-based deploys. Kubernetes core images pinned por digest. GitOps community (Argo, Flux) advocate digest pinning. AWS ECR IMMUTABLE feature launched 2020. Harbor immutability rules added 1.9 (2019).

questions.scenario: Tu equipo debate base image: Ubuntu (400MB, familiar), Alpine (5MB, minimal), Debian slim (30MB, middle), Distroless (variable, minimal + secure), Wolfi/Chainguard (minimal + zero-CVE).
questions.question: ¿Qué criteria usar para elegir base image?

options.text: Attack surface: fewer packages = fewer CVEs = less exposure. Distroless o Chainguard Wolfi tienen ~0 CVEs por design. Ubuntu tiene 100+ CVEs typical (mostly low, but still). En workloads sensibles, minimal base is huge win.
options.why: Correcto. Attack surface reduction fundamental. Cada package instalado es potential vulnerability. Distroless/Wolfi minimizan drastically.

options.text: Size: base size directly affects deploy speed, storage cost, cold start. 5MB Alpine vs 400MB Ubuntu = 80x factor. Multiplicado por número de images/deployments/regions = significant cost.
options.why: Correcto. Size matters especially en K8s (each node pulls each image). Cold start times — 400MB pull toma 30-60s, 5MB toma 1s.

options.text: Compatibility: Alpine usa musl libc (not glibc). Some compiled binaries (Node native modules, Python C extensions) may fail. Ubuntu/Debian usan glibc — universal compatibility. Distroless glibc-based works for most.
options.why: Correcto. Musl vs glibc real issue. Sharp (Node image processing) infamous en Alpine. NumPy pip wheels not always Alpine-compat. Test extensively si Alpine.

options.text: Update cadence: base image tiene CVEs fixed regularmente. Elige base que se update frecuentemente. Ubuntu, Debian slim update semanal. Alpine similar. Distroless Google-managed. Wolfi (Chainguard) daily updates.
options.why: Correcto. Stale bases = accumulating CVEs. Rebuild regularly (weekly?) para pull latest patched base. CI job: 'rebuild all images with latest bases'.

options.text: Base image selection no importa — todas son iguales.
options.why: Falso — impact huge en security, cost, performance.

questions.explanation:
Base image comparison:

(1) UBUNTU (200-400MB): Familiar, complete distribution. Package manager (apt). Debug tools included. Many CVEs (typical 100+ low/medium). Slow to pull, big storage.

(2) DEBIAN SLIM (30-70MB): Debian sin extras (docs, tools). Still complete-ish. Similar packages to Ubuntu. Faster pull. Good balance.

(3) ALPINE (5MB base): Minimal, musl libc. apk package manager. Very small. Compatibility issues con native modules. Popular pero fading (musl issues persist).

(4) DISTROLESS (Google, ~5-50MB depending): No shell, no package manager. Static or dynamic variants. Glibc-based. Multi-language support. Excellent security. Debug challenging.

(5) SCRATCH (0 bytes): Truly empty. For static binaries (Go, Rust, C static). Absolute minimum. Debug impossible.

(6) CHAINGUARD IMAGES / WOLFI (variable): Minimal, glibc-based, daily rebuilds, signed, SBOM. Enterprise-focused. Growing adoption.

(7) UBI (Red Hat Universal Base Image): RHEL-based. Enterprise compliance-friendly. Larger than Alpine, smaller than Ubuntu.

Decision matrix:
- STATIC BINARY (Go, Rust) → scratch or distroless/static.
- SIMPLE APP + WANT SHELL → Alpine or Debian slim.
- COMPLEX APP + COMPATIBILITY IMPORTANT → Debian slim.
- HIGH SECURITY REQUIREMENTS → Distroless or Chainguard.
- LEGACY / FAMILIAR OPS → Ubuntu.
- REGULATED / ENTERPRISE → UBI or Chainguard.

Monitoring base: (1) trivy image <base>:tag para count CVEs. (2) SBOM del base. (3) Update policy — how often rebuild? (4) Vendor support — vendor patches?

Pro tip: multi-stage — builder can be Ubuntu (dev tools), runtime distroless (security). Best of both.
questions.realWorld: Alpine dominant en 2015-2020 pero musl issues cause migration back. Distroless (Google) launched 2017. Chainguard (2022+) founded by Kubernetes/Sigstore founders — 'secure by default' base images. Wolfi (Chainguard's undistro) launched 2022. En 2024, Chainguard Images gaining big enterprise adoption.

questions.scenario: Tus containers están 'seguros' en build (scan passed), pero necesitas detectar attack DURANTE runtime (attacker exploits a live vulnerability, ejecuta comando raro).
questions.question: ¿Qué es Falco y qué provee?

options.text: Falco (CNCF Graduated): runtime security tool que monitorea syscalls del kernel + K8s API events + logs. Detecta comportamientos anómalos: unexpected shell in container, sensitive file read (/etc/passwd), network to unexpected destination, privilege escalation, container escape attempts, cryptomining. Rules-based (YAML). Alerts via webhook, Slack, PagerDuty. Original by Sysdig, donated to CNCF. Uses eBPF (o kernel module) para syscall inspection.
options.why: Correcto. Falco is defacto standard runtime security. CNCF Graduated 2024. Widely deployed. eBPF-based (modern) — kernel-level visibility sin high overhead.

options.text: Falco es scanner de images.
options.why: Falso — Trivy, Grype son scanners (static). Falco es runtime (dynamic).

options.text: Falco reemplaza firewalls.
options.why: Falso — complementa. Firewalls son network-level, Falco es syscall/behavior-level.

options.text: Falco es paid-only.
options.why: Falso — CNCF open source. Sysdig ofrece commercial version con additional features.

questions.explanation:
Falco example rules:
```yaml
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: Shell was spawned in a container
  condition: >
    container.id != host
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, ash)
    and proc.tty != 0
  output: >
    Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.name)
  priority: WARNING

- rule: Read sensitive file
  desc: Read of /etc/shadow or similar
  condition: >
    open_read and container
    and (fd.name = /etc/shadow or fd.name = /etc/passwd)
  output: 'Sensitive file read: %fd.name in %container.name'
  priority: CRITICAL
```

Deployment: (1) DaemonSet en K8s — one pod per node. Uses eBPF probe o kernel module (privileged). (2) Falco events → falcosidekick → destinations (Slack, PagerDuty, S3, Kafka). (3) Prometheus metrics.

Rules: (1) Built-in default set — hundreds of rules covering common attacks. (2) Custom rules for your specific env. (3) Rules from community (falco-project/rules). (4) Machine-learning-based rules (Sysdig Secure commercial).

eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter): kernel technology para run sandboxed programs. Falco uses to hook syscalls without kernel module. Modern approach. Alternative: legacy kernel module (still supported).

Use cases: (1) Cryptomining detection — process patterns matching XMRig, minerd. (2) Container escape attempts — mount /host, access /proc/1/root. (3) Reverse shell — process piping to network socket. (4) Privilege escalation — setuid syscall from container. (5) K8s API abuse — anomalous API calls.

Tradeoffs: (1) Alert volume — dev environments generate many 'anomalies'. Tuning needed. (2) Rule maintenance — custom rules per app. (3) Response — alert only vs auto-block. Falco alerts; blocking is manual/other tools (Kyverno, admission controllers).

Alternatives: (1) Aqua Security enforcement. (2) Sysdig Secure (commercial). (3) Tetragon (Isovalent, Cilium team) — eBPF-based, similar. (4) Kubescape — CNCF, more posture management. (5) Datadog Cloud Security Management.
questions.realWorld: Falco started 2016 (Sysdig). CNCF Incubating 2018, Graduated 2024. Widely deployed en enterprise K8s. Tetragon (2022+, Cilium team) modern eBPF alternative. En 2023, Kubescape (ARMO, CNCF) gaining traction para posture + runtime.

questions.scenario: Tu K8s cluster tiene pods que corren como root, con host network, con hostPath mounts. Security team demanda hardening.
questions.question: ¿Qué son Pod Security Standards (PSS) y cómo aplicarlos?

options.text: Pod Security Standards (PSS): 3 profiles de restricciones de K8s pods. (1) PRIVILEGED — sin restricciones (legacy). (2) BASELINE — minimum acceptable (deny known dangerous features). (3) RESTRICTED — heavily hardened, current best practices. Enforce via Pod Security Admission controller (PSA, replaces deprecated PodSecurityPolicy). Levels: enforce (block), audit (log), warn (message). Apply per namespace via labels.
options.why: Correcto. PSS + PSA es el standard K8s moderno (1.25+ GA, PSP deprecated). Simple, layered enforcement.

options.text: PSS es una feature deprecated.
options.why: Falso — PSA es GA en K8s 1.25 (2022). PodSecurityPolicy (predecessor) fue deprecated.

options.text: PSS solo aplica a Google Kubernetes Engine.
options.why: Falso — feature core de K8s.

options.text: Pod Security requires third-party tools.
options.why: PSS is built-in K8s. Third-party (OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) offer más flexibility pero PSS suffices para most.

questions.explanation:
PSS profiles detail:

PRIVILEGED: sin restricciones. Todos los features Kubernetes disponibles. Solo para system pods (kube-system components).

BASELINE: prevent known escalations. Restricts: (1) hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC. (2) hostPath volumes (with exceptions). (3) privileged containers. (4) Uso de capabilities SYS_ADMIN, etc. (5) hostProcess (Windows). Reasonable para most workloads.

RESTRICTED: heavily hardened. Requires: (1) runAsNonRoot: true. (2) allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. (3) capabilities.drop: [ALL]. (4) seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault. (5) readOnlyRootFilesystem preferred. (6) No hostPath, hostNetwork, etc. Strong security posture.

Enforcement modes:
- enforce — block violating pods.
- audit — log to audit log.
- warn — return warning to kubectl output.

Application via namespace label:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: myapp
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.28
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
```

Migration path: (1) Start with warn/audit on baseline. Log violations. (2) Fix violations. (3) Move to enforce baseline. (4) Repeat with restricted. Progressive.

History: (1) PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) — original K8s security. Complex, extremely flexible, hard to manage. Deprecated 1.21, removed 1.25. (2) Pod Security Admission (PSA) — replacement. Opinionated, simpler.

Beyond PSS — OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno: more flexible policy engines. Custom rules ('all images must be from Harbor', 'all pods must have resource limits', 'no LoadBalancer services in this namespace'). PSS covers common cases; Gatekeeper/Kyverno for custom.

Admission controllers: (1) PSA — built-in. (2) OPA Gatekeeper — Rego language. (3) Kyverno — YAML-based, K8s-native. (4) Kubewarden — WebAssembly policies. Multiple can coexist.
questions.realWorld: PSP deprecated K8s 1.21 (2021), removed 1.25 (2022). PSA GA 1.25. Kyverno gaining fast adoption over Gatekeeper (simpler UX). En 2023, Chainguard Enforce for K8s admission control gaining enterprise traction. Falco/Tetragon complement PSS for runtime.

questions.scenario: En tu K8s cluster, pod A puede llamar a cualquier otro pod, incluso DB de otro team. Un attacker que compromise pod A tiene acceso lateral a todo.
questions.question: ¿Qué son Network Policies en K8s?

options.text: NetworkPolicy: K8s resource que define reglas de traffic ingress/egress a pods. Por default K8s allows all-to-all — cualquier pod puede talk to cualquier otro. NetworkPolicy switches a deny-by-default cuando aplica. Selectors por labels (podSelector, namespaceSelector). Requires CNI plugin que support NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Weave; NOT flannel). Enables microsegmentation — 'frontend pods pueden hablar a backend, backend a DB, nothing else'.
options.why: Correcto. Fundamental K8s security control. Muchos clusters no configuran NetworkPolicies — huge miss. Zero-trust en cluster requires them.

options.text: K8s previene tráfico automáticamente.
options.why: Falso — default es all allow. Debes create policies explícitamente.

options.text: NetworkPolicy es lo mismo que firewall externo.
options.why: Complementa firewall externo. NetworkPolicy es INTRA-cluster (pod-to-pod). Firewall es cluster-boundary.

options.text: Todos los CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy.
options.why: Falso — flannel default no. Calico, Cilium, Weave sí. Verify tu CNI.

questions.explanation:
Ejemplo NetworkPolicy:
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-api
  namespace: myapp
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: frontend
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: database
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432
    - to: []  # allow DNS to any
      ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
```

Default deny (recommended baseline):
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: myapp
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
```
Deny todo. Otras NetworkPolicies añaden allowances.

Selector types: (1) podSelector — pods en mismo namespace matching labels. (2) namespaceSelector — pods en namespaces matching labels. (3) ipBlock — CIDR ranges. Para external services o cross-cluster.

Common patterns: (1) Default deny + selective allows. Zero-trust posture. (2) Namespace-scoped — 'only pods in ns X can talk to pods in ns X'. (3) Egress restrictions — 'these pods can only egress to specific services'. (4) DNS carve-out — always allow port 53 UDP.

Advanced: Cilium adds L7 policies (HTTP methods, paths). Cilium/Istio service mesh adds mTLS, more granular. NetworkPolicy L3/L4 only — no HTTP semantics.

Debugging: (1) 'kubectl describe netpol'. (2) Cilium 'hubble' UI. (3) Calico 'calicoctl'. (4) Try curl from pod y trace. (5) Common: forgot DNS egress → nothing resolves. (6) Common: label mismatch — policy applies to wrong pods.

How it works internally: CNI plugin implements iptables/ipvs/eBPF rules to enforce. Applied per node. K8s API just stores the rules; CNI enforces.
questions.realWorld: Cilium (2015+, CNCF Graduated) is dominant CNI, eBPF-based. Calico similar traction. Flannel + Calico combos común. Netflix uses Calico. Google Anthos uses Cilium. Zero-trust architecture con NetworkPolicies + mTLS (Istio/Linkerd) es enterprise standard 2024.

questions.scenario: Tu pod corre como root y con full capabilities. Tu security scan flags esto. Debes hardening el pod spec.
questions.question: ¿Qué es securityContext en K8s y qué configurar?

options.text: runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000 — pod no puede correr como root. Restricted PSS requires this. Debe combinar con Dockerfile 'USER nonroot' o image que tenga non-root user.
options.why: Correcto. Baseline security. K8s can enforce, no depende solo del Dockerfile.

options.text: capabilities.drop: [ALL] + capabilities.add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE] — remove all capabilities, add back only needed. Least privilege. Sin capabilities dropping, container puede tener CAP_SYS_ADMIN implícito (dangerous).
options.why: Correcto. Capabilities son Linux root split. Container por default hereda muchas. Drop ALL + add solo needed = principle of least privilege.

options.text: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — root filesystem del container inmutable. Writes fallan. App usa volumes/emptyDir para paths que necesitan writes (logs, tmp). Prevents malicious modification of binaries en runtime.
options.why: Correcto. Container escape scenarios usually involve write to filesystem. Read-only bloquea. App may need adjustments (tmpfs para /tmp).

options.text: seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault — restricts kernel syscalls the container can make. RuntimeDefault (Docker/containerd default) blocks ~40 dangerous syscalls (kexec, mount, etc.). Custom seccomp profiles can be even more strict.
options.why: Correcto. Seccomp is powerful sandboxing. Default profile is a good baseline. Custom profiles for further hardening (though complex to maintain).

options.text: securityContext es opcional y sin efecto.
options.why: Falso — es fundamental para K8s security. Restricted PSS requires several fields.

questions.explanation:
Full hardened example:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
    fsGroup: 2000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:v1
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: [ALL]
          add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]  # solo si necesita
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /app/cache
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir: {}
    - name: cache
      emptyDir: {}
```

Campos importantes:

Pod-level securityContext: (1) runAsNonRoot — pod cannot run as UID 0. (2) runAsUser, runAsGroup — specific UID/GID. (3) fsGroup — GID for volume ownership. (4) supplementalGroups. (5) seccompProfile. (6) sysctls — kernel params.

Container-level: (1) capabilities.drop/add. (2) allowPrivilegeEscalation: false — cannot gain new capabilities via setuid. (3) privileged: false — no --privileged (default). (4) readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. (5) runAsUser (override pod-level). (6) seccompProfile (override).

Linux capabilities (partial list): (1) NET_ADMIN — network config. (2) NET_BIND_SERVICE — bind privileged ports (<1024). (3) SYS_ADMIN — many admin ops (dangerous). (4) SYS_TIME — set system time. (5) SETUID/SETGID. (6) DAC_OVERRIDE — bypass permission checks. Total: 40+. Container defaults have ~14. Drop all + add specific = safest.

Common capabilities needed: (1) NET_BIND_SERVICE — HTTP server on port 80. Not needed if binding >1024. (2) CHOWN — chown files (some entrypoint scripts). (3) SETUID/SETGID — some apps switch users. Most apps: none needed.

Debugging security context issues: (1) 'kubectl describe pod' shows applied SC. (2) Test with fewer restrictions, add back gradually. (3) Watch for permission errors en logs. (4) Runtime tools (Falco, audit logs) show blocked ops.
questions.realWorld: Kubernetes 1.19+ made seccompProfile GA. GKE Autopilot, Red Hat OpenShift enforce restricted PSS by default. En 2023, Kyverno added policy generation from vulnerability scans. Chainguard workload identity + hardened pods para production readiness. Restricted PSS + no bit CVEs = good posture.

questions.scenario: Se anuncia una CVE crítica en OpenSSL. Tienes 200 images corriendo en prod. ¿Cómo saber cuáles afectados y remediation?
questions.question: ¿Cómo gestionar CVEs en escala a nivel org?

options.text: SBOM inventory: para cada image en producción, tienes un SBOM. Query 'qué images contain openssl vX.Y' — instant list de affected. Sin SBOMs, tienes que scan every image manually (slow).
options.why: Correcto. SBOM inventory es lo que permite respond fast. Log4Shell taught many orgs esta lección — sin SBOM, days de discovery.

options.text: Continuous scanning: no solo scan en CI (build time). Scan images IN registry regularly (weekly). Trivy, Grype, Sysdig soportan. New CVEs appear all the time; static scan at build ages fast.
options.why: Correcto. CVEs se descubren daily. Un image scan clean 3 semanas atrás puede tener critical CVE ahora. Continuous scanning catches.

options.text: Base image auto-update: pipelines automáticos (Renovate, Dependabot) que create PRs cuando base image tiene update. CI rebuilds. Deploy pipelines automatizan re-releasing. Reduces exposure time.
options.why: Correcto. Un CVE fix en base image sirve nada si tus images no re-build. Automation clave para responsiveness.

options.text: Prioritization: no todos CVE críticos son URGENT en tu contexto. Contextual factors: is the vulnerable code path used? Is service exposed to internet? Reachability analysis (Trivy VEX, Endor Labs). Focus on real risk, not just CVSS score.
options.why: Correcto. Alert fatigue is real. 1000 CVEs medium = ignored. Tools con reachability analysis reduce noise — 'this CVE is in a code path you don't use, mark not-affected'.

options.text: Ignorar CVEs bajos permanentemente.
options.why: Falso — low CVEs are still real. Track y address con lower priority. Some low CVEs chain into higher-severity attacks.

questions.explanation:
CVE management program: (1) INVENTORY — know what runs in prod. SBOMs help. (2) SCAN — continuous, not just CI. (3) PRIORITIZE — CVSS + reachability + exploitability + business impact. (4) REMEDIATE — patch (upgrade dep), mitigate (WAF, config), or accept + document. (5) TRACK — SLA per severity. (6) VERIFY — confirm remediation actually applied.

SLAs typical: (1) Critical (CVSS 9-10) — patch within 24-72h. (2) High (7-8.9) — within 7-14 days. (3) Medium (4-6.9) — 30-90 days. (4) Low — quarterly.

Remediation options: (1) Upgrade — bump dep to fixed version. Preferred. (2) Backport patch — for old versions. (3) Replace dep — use alternative. (4) Mitigate — WAF rule, config change, feature flag disable. Not fix but reduces risk. (5) Accept — document justification, monitor. (6) Isolate — network isolation, minimize exposure.

Tools: (1) Snyk — commercial, dev-focused. Reachability analysis. (2) Grype/Syft — Anchore, open source. (3) Trivy — open source. (4) Sysdig Secure — commercial, runtime + build. (5) Endor Labs — reachability focus. (6) GitHub Dependabot — for repos. Dependabot alerts, security advisories.

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange): SBOM-adjacent format for 'this CVE does NOT affect our product because X'. Attach to SBOMs. Reduces false positive noise. Growing adoption.

Registries + scanning: (1) Harbor scans on push, blocks pull based on policy. (2) ECR image scanning built-in. (3) Docker Scout. Alerts, dashboards.

Case Log4Shell (Dec 2021): (1) Discovery: many orgs didn't have SBOM inventory. (2) Manual scanning of images took days. (3) Some found in TRANSITIVE deps of application deps. (4) Patch involved: upgrading log4j, restarting apps. (5) Continuous new attacks discovered — CVEs kept coming. Weeks of work. Post-Log4Shell, SBOMs adopted broadly.
questions.realWorld: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) December 2021 — most impactful CVE ever. Hundreds of thousands affected. Post-event: US EO 14028 (2021) accelerated SBOM. Government contracts require SBOMs. Chainguard Images promise: 'zero known CVEs at time of build'. Continuous rebuilds keep it that way.

questions.scenario: Auditor pregunta: 'Cómo garantizas que el binary desplegado fue realmente buildeado desde el commit que dices?'. Empresa quiere adoptar SLSA.
questions.question: ¿Qué es SLSA y cuáles son sus niveles?

options.text: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, se pronuncia 'salsa'): framework de Google/OpenSSF para supply chain security. Niveles L1-L4. L1: documentation of build process. L2: hosted build service + tampering resistance. L3: source y build integrity, non-forgeable provenance. L4: two-party review, hermetic reproducible builds. Los niveles definen QUÉ tan confiable es el proceso de build. Provenance attestation firma 'este artifact fue buildeado desde este source, con este comando, en este builder'.
options.why: Correcto. SLSA es el standard emergente para supply chain security. Google/OpenSSF. Adopted by CNCF (Kubernetes L3), by federal software (US EO).

options.text: SLSA es lo mismo que CVE scanning.
options.why: Diferentes. SLSA es sobre BUILD PROCESS integrity. CVE es sobre known vulnerabilities. Complementarios.

options.text: SLSA solo aplica a OSS.
options.why: Falso — applies to any software artifact production.

options.text: SLSA es un producto de Google.
options.why: Framework abierto, contributed by Google. Now under OpenSSF (Linux Foundation).

questions.explanation:
SLSA levels detalle:

LEVEL 1: (1) Build process is documented. (2) Provenance attestation exists (metadata about build). Basic accountability.

LEVEL 2: L1 + (1) Version-controlled source. (2) Hosted build service (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Google Cloud Build). Provenance is authenticated (signed). Prevents casual tampering.

LEVEL 3: L2 + (1) Source and build are non-forgeable (secure storage, review). (2) Provenance is hermetic (build inputs fully specified). (3) Build service is isolated. Prevents insider attacks.

LEVEL 4: L3 + (1) Two-party review of all changes. (2) Hermetic + reproducible builds (same input → same output byte-by-byte). Highest trust.

Provenance format:
```json
{
  "buildDefinition": {
    "buildType": "https://github.com/actions/runner",
    "externalParameters": { "workflow": "build.yml", "ref": "refs/heads/main" },
    "resolvedDependencies": [{"uri": "git+https://...", "digest": "sha1:abc"}]
  },
  "runDetails": {
    "builder": {"id": "https://github.com/actions/runner"},
    "metadata": {"invocationId": "..."}
  }
}
```

Verification: consumers verify provenance before deploying: (1) Provenance signed by trusted builder. (2) Source matches expected repo/commit. (3) Build parameters expected.

Tools: (1) SLSA Verifier (Google) — verify provenance attestations. (2) sigstore/cosign attest — sign attestations. (3) GitHub Actions provenance (2023+) — auto-generated. (4) tekton chains — Tekton pipelines with SLSA. (5) Docker Buildx SLSA provenance (2023+).

GitHub Actions example (workflow):
```yaml
- name: Generate provenance
  uses: slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/generator_container_slsa3.yml@v1.9.0
  with:
    image: myapp
    digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
    registry-username: ${{ github.actor }}
  secrets:
    registry-password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```
Generates SLSA L3 provenance.

Key use cases: (1) Verify what's deployed matches source. (2) Prevent 'malicious insider' — changes require review. (3) Reproducible builds allow independent verification. (4) Chain of trust — provenance links source → build → artifact → deploy.
questions.realWorld: SLSA launched 2021 by Google, transferred to OpenSSF 2022. Kubernetes core reached SLSA L3 in 2023. NPM added SLSA support 2023. Google Cloud Build, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI all support SLSA. Post-SolarWinds (2020) heightened supply chain focus. US EO 14028 references SLSA.

questions.scenario: Tu CI necesita push images a ECR/GCR/GHCR. Static credentials en secrets es el pattern default. Un ingeniero senior menciona OIDC federation.
questions.question: ¿Cómo autenticar CI a registries de forma segura?

options.text: OIDC federation: CI provider (GHA, GitLab) emits OIDC JWT. Registry (o cloud provider hosting registry) verifies token, grants temporary credentials. No long-lived credentials. GHA + ECR con AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity es state-of-the-art. AWS, GCP, Azure all support.
options.why: Correcto. Best practice. Elimina long-lived credentials — main compromise vector.

options.text: Robot accounts (Harbor): accounts dedicated para automation. Limited scope (specific project, actions). Token-based. Rotable. Better than personal access tokens.
options.why: Correcto. Harbor robot accounts — not tied to personal user, revocable, scope-limited. Similar concepts en other registries (deploy tokens en GitLab, machine accounts).

options.text: Credential helpers: docker-credential-helper plugins que fetch credentials dynamically desde vault (AWS credential helper, gcp-auth, azure-credential-helper). Docker daemon calls helper cuando needs auth. No static secrets en config.json.
options.why: Correcto. Credential helper pattern excellent para dev environments — automatic auth basada en cloud IAM. Producción CI similarmente.

options.text: GitHub Actions con GHCR + GITHUB_TOKEN: automatic. Workflow tiene GITHUB_TOKEN con permission a GHCR. 'permissions: packages: write'. No configurar credentials manually.
options.why: Correcto. GHCR + GHA integration is smooth. No separate credentials, uses ambient GITHUB_TOKEN. Similar en GitLab (CI_JOB_TOKEN).

options.text: Hardcodear passwords en el Dockerfile.
options.why: Anti-patrón crítico. Nunca.

questions.explanation:
Auth patterns por registry:

DOCKER HUB: (1) Docker Hub username + password. (2) Personal Access Token (PAT) — recommended over password. (3) Organization tokens. Static creds en CI secret.

ECR (AWS): (1) IAM user access key + secret (static, avoid). (2) IAM role + AssumeRole. (3) OIDC federation from CI (GHA + AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity). Recommended.

GCR/Artifact Registry (GCP): (1) Service account JSON key (static, avoid). (2) Workload Identity Federation con OIDC. (3) Local: 'gcloud auth configure-docker'. In K8s: Workload Identity.

ACR (Azure): (1) Service Principal. (2) Managed Identity. (3) OIDC federation con Azure AD.

GHCR: (1) Personal Access Token (classic). (2) GITHUB_TOKEN en GHA workflows (automatic). (3) Fine-grained PAT.

HARBOR: (1) User accounts (static). (2) Robot accounts. (3) OIDC integration (external IdP). (4) LDAP integration.

JFrog Artifactory: (1) API keys. (2) Access tokens. (3) OIDC integration.

Docker config.json:
```json
{
  "auths": {
    "registry.example.com": {
      "auth": "base64encoded_user:pass"
    }
  },
  "credsStore": "osxkeychain"  // or ecr-login, gcloud, etc.
}
```
CredsStore plugin fetches credentials dynamically.

ECR-specific: (1) 'aws ecr get-login-password | docker login' — token-based, short-lived (12h). (2) IAM permission ecr:GetAuthorizationToken. (3) K8s EKS uses IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) — pod's ServiceAccount linked to IAM role — automatic.

Best practices: (1) Prefer OIDC/workload identity para CI. (2) Rotate any static credentials regularly. (3) Least privilege — CI role can push to specific repo, not entire registry. (4) Audit logs — monitor auth events for anomalies. (5) MFA on personal accounts.
questions.realWorld: In 2020, Codecov breach exposed CI credentials — accelerated OIDC federation adoption. GHA + ECR OIDC (2021+) el pattern estándar. GitLab OIDC en CI (2022+). Docker Hub 2FA now recommended (2022+). En 2023, GitHub tightened PAT security defaults.

questions.scenario: Un attacker compromise una app en un container. Su goal: escape del container y controlar el host. ¿Qué vectors defenders should know?
questions.question: ¿Cuáles son los principales container escape vectors?

options.text: Privileged container: '--privileged' flag da acceso a todos devices, capabilities, kernel features. Basically root en host. Legitimate uses raros (some CI runners). Never for regular workloads. K8s: 'privileged: true' en securityContext.
options.why: Correcto. Privileged es easy escape. Container puede mount /dev/sda, edit host filesystem. Prod workloads never privileged.

options.text: hostPath volume mounting /: 'volumes: hostPath: path: /'. Container writes to host filesystem. Add SSH key to host's authorized_keys. Full host takeover. Restricted PSS blocks hostPath (mostly). Use with care.
options.why: Correcto. hostPath es 'legal' escape. Legit uses (log collectors, monitoring agents) with strict scope. Never mount /.

options.text: Docker socket exposure: mount /var/run/docker.sock en container. Container puede llamar Docker API — spawn new containers, mount host paths, etc. Full host control. 'DinD' pattern (Docker in Docker for CI) common — dangerous if untrusted code runs.
options.why: Correcto. Socket exposure = root del host. Common en CI (Docker builds), analytics agents. Untrusted code + docker.sock = catastrophe.

options.text: Kernel vulnerabilities: runc CVE-2019-5736 (rewritten runc binary from container). CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe — write to any file). Kernel vulns bypass container isolation completely. Mitigation: patched kernels, seccomp, non-root, gVisor.
options.why: Correcto. Kernel exploits are the ultimate escape. Container isolation depends on kernel — if kernel is compromised, isolation broken. Kernel patching is critical.

options.text: Los containers son unhackeables.
options.why: Falso — multiple documented escapes. Isolation is strong pero not perfect. Defense-in-depth needed.

questions.explanation:
Escape vectors detailed:

(1) PRIVILEGED CONTAINER — full escape. Access to host devices, kernel modules, all capabilities. Rarely legitimate. K8s Restricted PSS blocks.

(2) HOST NAMESPACE SHARING — hostNetwork (see host's network), hostPID (see host processes, kill them), hostIPC. Reduces isolation.

(3) HOSTPATH MOUNTS — direct filesystem access. Escapes obvious (mount /, mount /etc). More subtle: mount /var/log (rewrite logs to hide), mount /proc/1/root (host filesystem indirectly).

(4) DOCKER SOCKET — direct Docker API access from container. Common in CI (docker builds). Alternatives: DinD (isolated Docker daemon in container — safer if properly configured), Buildkit rootless, Kaniko (no daemon).

(5) DANGEROUS CAPABILITIES — CAP_SYS_ADMIN allows mount syscalls (escape), CAP_SYS_PTRACE (attach to host processes), CAP_NET_ADMIN (kernel routing). Drop all + add only needed.

(6) KERNEL EXPLOITS — highly technical. Requires unpatched kernel. Examples: runc CVE-2019-5736, Dirty Pipe (2022), Symlink races. Mitigation: patch kernels, use seccomp to block syscalls, gVisor (userspace kernel — extra isolation).

(7) SETUID BINARIES — inside container, a setuid binary could escalate if capabilities allow. AllowPrivilegeEscalation: false + drop capabilities blocks.

(8) SERVICE ACCOUNT TOKENS — K8s SA JWT auto-mounted. If container has SA with cluster-admin, use kubectl to schedule new pod on host with privileged. Fix: minimize SA permissions, disable auto-mount when not needed.

(9) LATERAL MOVEMENT — from compromised container, exploit weak K8s NetworkPolicies to reach other services (DB, internal APIs). Zero-trust network is defense.

Defenses (layered): (1) Pod Security Restricted profile. (2) Non-root, no privileged. (3) Drop capabilities, seccomp. (4) NetworkPolicies (segmentation). (5) Runtime monitoring (Falco, Tetragon). (6) Patched kernels. (7) Minimal images (reduce attack surface). (8) Consider gVisor or Kata Containers for high-security workloads (VM-like isolation).

Runtime detection: Falco rules detect: unexpected shell, sensitive file read, mount syscall in container, execve of /bin/bash from odd process. Alert on these.
questions.realWorld: runc CVE-2019-5736 (Adam Iwaniuk, Borys Popławski) — first major container escape at scale. Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195), Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) — kernel issues bypassing container isolation. gVisor (Google) — userspace kernel for extra isolation. Kata Containers — VMs disguised as containers. Both trade performance for security.

questions.scenario: Tu security policy dice: 'solo images signed by trusted publishers deploy en prod'. K8s no verifica firmas por default. ¿Cómo enforce?
questions.question: ¿Cómo enforce signature verification en K8s cluster?

options.text: Admission controllers con verify: Kyverno, Sigstore Policy Controller (formerly Cosigned), Connaisseur, Ratify. Interceptan Pod creation, verifican signature del image contra trusted keys/identities. Reject si no signed correctamente. Deployment gate a runtime.
options.why: Correcto. Admission controllers son THE way de enforce policy en K8s. Multiple options. Kyverno gaining fast adoption por simple YAML config.

options.text: Kyverno policy example: verify images matching pattern signed by specific OIDC identity (ej. GitHub Actions from myorg/*). Rejects otherwise. Fine-grained: production namespace estricto, dev namespace permissive.
options.why: Correcto. Kyverno syntax for verifyImages is clean. Supports keyless (OIDC), keyed, and multiple attestors.

options.text: Verify attestations no solo images: cosign attest para SBOM, vulnerability scans, SLSA provenance. Policy requires attestations verified before deploy — proves builder identity, source SHA, dep list, no critical CVEs.
options.why: Correcto. Signatures verifican WHO signed. Attestations verifican WHAT was built and PROPERTIES (SBOM, scan). Full supply chain verification requires attestations.

options.text: Notary v2 / notation project: alternative to cosign. OCI-native signature standard. Similar goals, distinct implementation. Growing support en registries.
options.why: Correcto. Notary v2 (renamed notation) es CNCF project. cosign popular pero notation es also valid alternative. Some enterprise registries prefer notation.

options.text: K8s verifica firmas automaticamente sin config.
options.why: Falso — K8s por default no verifica image signatures. Requires admission controller or ImagePolicyWebhook.

questions.explanation:
Kyverno signature verification example:
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-signed-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30
  rules:
    - name: verify-image-cosign
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences:
            - 'ghcr.io/myorg/*'
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    subject: 'https://github.com/myorg/*/.github/workflows/*'
                    issuer: 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com'
                    rekor:
                      url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
```
Enforce: any Pod using ghcr.io/myorg/* image must be signed by a GHA workflow in myorg/*.

Sigstore Policy Controller: dedicated tool para cosign policies. Similar functionality, cosign-native.

Attestation verification example (Kyverno):
```yaml
verifyImages:
  - imageReferences: ['*']
    attestations:
      - predicateType: https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2
        attestors:
          - entries:
              - keyless:
                  subject: '...'
        conditions:
          - all:
              - key: '{{ builder.id }}'
                operator: Equals
                value: 'https://github.com/actions/runner'
```
Requires SLSA provenance signed by expected builder.

Tradeoffs: (1) Availability — Rekor down = verification fails. Cached policies mitigate. (2) Bootstrapping — infrastructure to sign, keys, OIDC setup. Investment. (3) Emergency deploys — mecanismo para bypass en incident (with audit). (4) Third-party images — do they sign? If not, exception list o mirror + sign yourself.

Signing pipeline (build phase): (1) CI builds image. (2) Push to registry. (3) cosign sign image (with OIDC or key). (4) cosign attest SBOM, scan results, provenance. (5) Verify signatures immediately (test).

Production workflow: (1) Deploy manifest referring image. (2) Admission controller intercepts. (3) Fetches signature from registry (or Rekor). (4) Verifies against policy. (5) Allow or deny.

Monitoring: (1) Metrics — % of pods that verify. (2) Alerts on denials. (3) Audit trail — kubectl logs -n kyverno.
questions.realWorld: Sigstore Policy Controller (formerly Cosigned) launched by Sigstore project. Kyverno CNCF Incubating, gaining big adoption. Notary v2 (Notation) launched under CNCF 2022. Chainguard Enforce commercial around policy enforcement. Kubernetes core images signed by cosign (2023+).

questions.scenario: Tu app usa DB password inyectado como env var. Cuando rotan el password: (a) env vars son immutables durante lifetime del pod; (b) app conectada con old password sigue conectada; (c) new connections requieren restart.
questions.question: ¿Cómo hacer rotation de secrets sin downtime?

options.text: Secrets como file mounts + reload: mount secret como file en /etc/secrets. Cambio en Secret se refleja en filesystem (K8s reloads mount). App detecta change (inotify watch o polling) y reloads config. No restart. Reload de connections in-flight con new credentials.
options.why: Correcto. File mounts do update (env vars don't). App needs to support reload signal (SIGHUP tradicional). Modern apps often built for this.

options.text: External secret managers + short-lived tokens: Vault, AWS Secrets Manager. App fetches secret at startup, refetches periodically (or on error). Secret manager rotates behind scenes. Never long-lived static secret en pod.
options.why: Correcto. Best pattern. External vault as source of truth. App implements refresh logic. Rotation transparent.

options.text: Dynamic secrets: Vault issues UNIQUE credentials para cada app instance con short TTL (15min). App renews before expiry. Compromised credentials tienen limited blast radius (short window). Complex setup pero excellent security posture.
options.why: Correcto. Vault dynamic secrets — DB, cloud creds, PKI. Each app gets unique short-lived credential. Rotation is inherent.

options.text: Sidecar container que fetches y writes secret to shared volume. Main app reads del volume. Sidecar refreshes periodically. Main app reloads. Vault Agent, Secrets Store CSI Driver — patterns comunes.
options.why: Correcto. Sidecar pattern separates concerns. Main app doesn't know about Vault, just reads /secrets/db-password. Sidecar maneja auth, refresh.

options.text: Restart todos pods cada rotation.
options.why: Funciona but downtime + churn. Not ideal para high-availability. Reload es mejor.

questions.explanation:
Rotation strategies:

(1) FILE MOUNT WITH RELOAD: K8s Secret mounted as file. K8s auto-updates file on Secret change. App uses fsnotify/inotify to detect + reload config. NGINX SIGHUP reload es classic ejemplo. Apps deben support graceful reload.

(2) ENV VARS: DO NOT auto-update en running pod. Solo new pods pick up new value. Requires pod restart. Simpler para app pero has downtime issue.

(3) EXTERNAL SECRETS: app calls Vault/AWS Secrets Manager on startup + periodically. HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager. K8s adjacencies: External Secrets Operator, Vault Sidecar, Secrets Store CSI Driver.

(4) DYNAMIC SECRETS: Vault issues unique credentials with lease. App renews lease before expiry. Vault revokes on lease end. Ex: Vault DB engine — issues MySQL user with 15min TTL. Rotation es inherent.

(5) SIDECAR PATTERN: Vault Agent Injector — inject sidecar into pods. Sidecar authenticates with Vault, writes secrets to emptyDir volume, refreshes. App reads from volume.

Secrets Store CSI Driver: (1) K8s standard. (2) Mount external secrets as volumes. (3) Supported providers: Vault, AWS, GCP, Azure. (4) Sync mode — creates K8s Secret from external. (5) Rotation via periodic reconciliation.

External Secrets Operator: (1) CRD-based. (2) External SecretStore reference. (3) K8s Secret populated from external. (4) Refresh interval. (5) Multi-provider support.

Rotation of DB creds (dynamic secrets ideal):
1. App calls Vault: 'give me DB creds'.
2. Vault creates fresh MySQL user, TTL 1h.
3. Vault returns creds to app.
4. App connects, works.
5. After 45min, app renews lease (still 45min renewal window).
6. If app dies without renewing, Vault revokes user at TTL expiry.
7. Compromised creds only usable within window.

This pattern avoids the rotation problem entirely — creds are ephemeral by design.

Alerts: monitor Vault/Secrets Manager rotation events. Alert on failed rotations. Track secrets not rotated for X days.
questions.realWorld: HashiCorp Vault dominates enterprise secrets management. AWS Secrets Manager + RDS auto-rotation lambdas common. GCP Secret Manager similar. External Secrets Operator (v1 GA 2023) rapid adoption. Secrets Store CSI Driver — K8s SIG-Auth. In 2020s, dynamic secrets increasingly adopted.

questions.scenario: Tu CTO menciona 'zero trust'. Actualmente asumen: firewall externo blocks bad guys, todo dentro del cluster es trusted. Post-Log4Shell, this assumption está roto.
questions.question: ¿Qué es zero-trust en el contexto de containers y qué layers implementarlo?

options.text: Zero-trust: 'never trust, always verify'. Asume that every request/actor could be malicious. Cada component verifies each other. No implicit trust based on network location. Applies within cluster, no solo boundary.
options.why: Correcto. Zero-trust es principio, no producto. Requiere layered implementation. Especialmente relevante post-massive breaches (Target 2013, SolarWinds 2020, Log4Shell 2021).

options.text: mTLS entre services: service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) auto-injects sidecar proxies que negotiate mTLS between services. Every service call is encrypted + authenticated. No unencrypted intra-cluster traffic. Compromise de un service no da access lateral to others sin cert.
options.why: Correcto. mTLS es foundation de zero-trust en K8s. Service mesh automates. Manual mTLS es tedious.

options.text: Workload identity + fine-grained IAM: each service has unique identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE, K8s ServiceAccount + Workload Identity). Access grants are per-workload, not per-cluster. 'Service A can call service B endpoint X' — enforced at policy layer.
options.why: Correcto. SPIFFE/SPIRE es estándar. Workload identity federated con cloud IAM. Fine-grained authz basado en identity.

options.text: Continuous verification: runtime monitoring (Falco, Tetragon) detects anomalies live. Combined con Vault dynamic secrets (short-lived credentials), continuous CVE scanning, cert rotation. Nothing is trusted 'forever' — periodic re-verification.
options.why: Correcto. Static assumptions are the enemy. Continuous verification of identity, credentials, compliance state. eBPF tools (Cilium, Tetragon) enable deep visibility.

options.text: Zero-trust significa deshacer todos los controles.
options.why: Opuesto — significa MÁS controles, más verification. 'Zero implicit trust', not 'zero controls'.

questions.explanation:
Zero-trust en K8s (layers):

(1) NETWORK — NetworkPolicies deny-by-default. Service mesh mTLS. No unencrypted intra-cluster.

(2) IDENTITY — SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity. K8s ServiceAccounts. Workload Identity Federation to cloud IAM.

(3) POLICY — Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper enforce compliance policies. Pod Security Standards Restricted. Admission control.

(4) SECRETS — Vault dynamic secrets. Short-lived credentials. Rotation without downtime.

(5) SUPPLY CHAIN — Signed images (cosign). SBOM. SLSA provenance. Admission control verifies signatures.

(6) RUNTIME — Falco/Tetragon detect anomalies. eBPF-based tracing. Automated response.

(7) OBSERVABILITY — Comprehensive logging (all API calls, auth events). SIEM aggregation. Correlation.

SPIFFE/SPIRE detail: SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone) — identity spec. SPIRE — implementation. Each workload gets SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document). JWT or X.509 form. Verifiable, short-lived. Cross-cluster + cross-cloud federation.

Service mesh comparison: (1) Istio — feature-rich, complex. (2) Linkerd — simpler, faster. (3) Consul Connect — HashiCorp. (4) Cilium Service Mesh — eBPF-based, no sidecar. (5) All support mTLS, traffic policies, observability.

Benchmarks common: (1) Mean time to detect (MTTD) — how fast do you know something anomalous? Zero-trust monitoring reduces to minutes. (2) Blast radius — if X is compromised, what can attacker reach? Zero-trust limits to X. (3) Cred rotation frequency — zero-trust: minutes/hours. Traditional: months.

Adoption path: (1) Start with NetworkPolicies (biggest bang for buck). (2) Deploy PSS Restricted. (3) Implement workload identity (Workload Identity Federation). (4) Service mesh with mTLS. (5) Vault dynamic secrets. (6) Signed images + admission control. (7) Runtime monitoring. Layer by layer, not big bang.

Culturally: 'zero trust' also means blameless postmortems, humility about security (assume you WILL be breached, plan detection + response), security as everyone's job (not just security team).
questions.realWorld: Google BeyondCorp (2014) — pioneer of zero-trust corporate networks. Cloudflare zero-trust products. En 2021, Biden EO required federal agencies move to zero-trust. CNCF 'Cloud Native Zero Trust Whitepaper' (2023). Chainguard's product suite built around zero-trust supply chain. Post-SolarWinds paradigm shift.
